say.text: Two patients, one burn pattern: the whole head and both whole legs. One is a 35-year-old man, the other a 2-year-old girl.
What decides which body chart you use?

choices.label: Adult rule of nines for both, legs are 18% each
Their age: a child's proportions differ
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the head first. Is a toddler's head the same share of the body as an adult's?
Tempting: the adult chart is the one you learned first, and most stems default to it. Why it fails: the rule of nines is built for adults.
In a child the head is about 18% and each leg about 14%, so adult figures overcount the legs and undercount the head. Age comes first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the belief to replace: the adult chart is not the default once the stem gives a child's age.

say.text: Yes. Age sets the chart. For an adult, the rule of nines gives the head 9% and each leg 18%. For a child, use the Lund and Browder chart, because the head is about 18% and each leg about 14%.
An adult with burns to the head and neck, the whole front of the trunk and the perineum.
Total TBSA by the adult rule of nines?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go region by region and give each one its figure. Which regions carry the 9s, and which carry the 18s?
Tempting: the perineum sits low on the trunk, so it feels like a trunk-sized share. Why it fails: that counts the perineum as 9%.
The perineum is 1%. Head and neck 9, anterior trunk 18, perineum 1 gives 28%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the perineum figure: it is the smallest value on the adult chart.

say.text: Tempting: the head is large, so it feels as if it should carry the 18. Why it fails: the adult head and neck is 9%; 18 belongs to a leg or a side of the trunk.
Head and neck 9, anterior trunk 18, perineum 1 gives 28%, not 37%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-anchor the head: 9% in an adult, 18% only in a toddler.

say.text: Yes. Head and neck 9, anterior trunk 18, perineum 1: 28%. Each arm is 9 and each leg 18, and the whole adult chart adds to 100.
No chart this time. In the adult rule of nines, how much does the perineum count?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of the perineum as a small patch between the thighs, not a whole side of the body. Which figure fits a small patch?
Tempting: the perineum sits between the body sides, and the sides carry 18. Why it fails: each 18 is a leg or one side of the trunk, not the perineum.
On the adult chart the perineum is 1%. The 18s belong to each leg and to the front and back of the trunk.
Tempting: a small area feels like a 9. Why it fails: 9% is the head and each arm, and the perineum is smaller than that.
The perineum is 1%. Your 9s belong to the head and each arm.
Yes. The perineum is 1%. Keep the total check in mind: head 9, each arm 9, front and back of the trunk 18 each, each leg 18, perineum 1. That sums to 100.
Put the two charts side by side. Adult: head 9%, each leg 18%. Child: head about 18%, each leg about 14%.
Toddler: big head, short legs. Adult: small head, long legs. The same burn adds up differently.
A 2-year-old has burns to the whole head and one whole leg.
Total TBSA on the child chart?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the head, which changes most with age. Is it a bigger or smaller share in a toddler? Then do the leg.
Tempting: the adult chart is the one in your head, so 9 and 18 feel safe. Why it fails: those are adult figures, and a toddler's head and legs differ.
Child figures: head about 18%, one leg about 14%. Adding them gives 32%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age first: on a child chart the head and legs are not the adult values.

say.text: Tempting: the child's head is right, and the leg feels like the usual 18. Why it fails: a child's leg is about 14%, so the adult leg figure overcounts.
Head about 18% plus one leg about 14% gives 32%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note that a child's leg is smaller than an adult's, and the 18 cannot be kept.

say.text: Yes. Head about 18% and one leg about 14% gives 32%. The child's proportions are why the Lund and Browder chart exists.
Scalds cover the head and both legs of a 2-year-old, and you need a TBSA estimate.
Which method do you use?

choices.label: Wallace rule of nines, adult values
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the stem's age changes in the figures. Then pick the chart that corrects for that.
Tempting: Wallace is the name tied to the rule of nines, so it sounds like the proper chart. Why it fails: the rule of nines is an adult chart.
In a 2-year-old the head and legs are not the adult values. The Lund and Browder chart corrects for age.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pick the chart by age, not by the name you remember.

say.text: Tempting: it is the default in most stems, so it feels safe. Why it fails: unchanged adult figures overcount a child's legs and undercount the head.
Age sets the chart. The Lund and Browder chart is built for a child's proportions.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so drop the default: once the stem gives a child's age, the adult chart is out.

say.text: Yes. The Lund and Browder chart corrects for age, so it is the one to use in a child. The rule of nines stays the adult chart.
Count only partial-thickness and full-thickness areas toward TBSA. Superficial erythema is not counted.
For small, patchy burns, the palm with fingers is about 1%, so a few spots can be counted by it.
Your final check. Which set of adult values adds up to 100%?
Totals for each pair: arms, legs, and the trunk front plus back.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Add each set up in your head, starting with the head and the perineum. Which set makes exactly 100?
Tempting: the head is a big region, and 18 feels like a head figure. Why it fails: in an adult the head and neck is 9.
Head 9, arms 18, trunk 36, legs 36, perineum 1 totals 100. Head 18 pushes the sum to 109.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the head: 18 is a child's head figure, not the adult's.

say.text: Tempting: the perineum is a small area, and 9 is the figure you remember most. Why it fails: 9 belongs to the head and each arm.
The adult perineum is 1%. With 9 instead, the total is 108, not 100.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so anchor the perineum: it is the single 1% on the adult chart.

say.text: Yes. Head 9, arms 18, trunk 36, legs 36, perineum 1: 100%. Run that total check every time you estimate.
For a child, switch to the Lund and Browder chart before you add anything up.
